text: This lesson is about one real cost problem, reasoned through carefully rather than measured with invented benchmark numbers. The question is simple: why does a nightly full reload that used to be fine suddenly start struggling to finish, even though nothing about the business changed?

Here's the uncomfortable shape of the Beginner project's pipeline, stated plainly. Every night, it reads the entire accumulated history in bronze-dot-sales-raw, rebuilds all of silver-dot-sales-clean from that history, and rebuilds all of Gold from that -- just to answer questions about one new day's worth of transactions. That's not a bug. It was the right call when the pipeline had only been running a few weeks.

You don't need a real benchmark to see where this goes -- the shape of the problem is enough. Picture a job that today reprocesses six months of accumulated history every night to add one new day's worth of transactions. Fast-forward, and that same job is now reprocessing closer to a year of history to add that exact same one new day. The new work never grew at all. Only the old work being redone every night did.

Say the core principle out loud, because it's the reason this whole chapter exists: in a full-reload design, runtime and compute cost scale with total accumulated history, not with what's actually new. Every month that passes without changing the design, the nightly job gets a little more expensive and takes a little longer, regardless of whether yesterday was a slow Tuesday or the busiest day of the year.

That has two real consequences. First, the batch window gets harder to hit -- if the job needs to finish before stores open, a runtime that keeps creeping upward eventually misses that window with zero change in actual daily volume. Second, cost keeps rising with no new value delivered -- every extra minute spent re-reading six-month-old transactions that haven't changed produces exactly the same Gold table as before. It's pure overhead, and it compounds the longer the design stays unchanged.

An incremental design breaks that link entirely. Once Bronze only reads files newer than the watermark, and Silver only merges in rows that are actually new, nightly cost tracks the size of yesterday's data, not the size of the whole table. A year from now, the nightly run looks almost exactly like it does today. Next lesson, you'll build the first real piece of that: the incremental Bronze ingestion itself, in actual PySpark.
